fetched_contents.text: A study on the standard setting, validity, and reliability of a standardized patient performance rating scale – student version Abstract Introduction The quality of the performances of standardized patients plays a significant role in the effectiveness of clinical skills education. Therefore, providing standardized patients with constant feedback is essential. It is especially important to get students’ perspectives immediately following their encounters with standardized patients. In the literature, there is no scale for use by students to evaluate the performance of standardized patients. Thus, the three main goals of this study were to: (1) develop a scale for use by students to evaluate the performance of standardized patients, (2) examine the psychometric properties of the scale, and (3) determine a cut-off score for the scale in a standard-setting Materials and methods Seven hundred and two medical students participated in the scale- development process, the pilot test, and the validation process, and seven educators took part in the standard-setting process. After the evaluation of content validity, construct validity was assessed via exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses. For the standard-setting study, the extended Angoff method was used. Results The exploratory factor analysis revealed that the scale had a single-factor structure, which was confirmed by confirmatory factor analysis. The Cronbach’s alpha internal consistency coefficient was 0.91. The scale consists of nine items. The cut-off score was determined to be 24.11/45, which represents the minimum acceptable standard for standardized patient performance. Conclusions Our study outlined the critical steps in developing a measurement tool and produced a valid and reliable scale that allows medical students to assess the performance of standardized patients immediately following their interaction with the standardized patient. This scale constitutes an important contribution to the literature as it provides a tool for standardized patient trainers to assess standardized patients’ weaknesses and help them improve their performance. KEY MESSAGES * Evaluation of SP performance is essential to ensure the educational quality of clinical skills training programs. * Students are the most relevant stakeholders to give feedback about SP performance immediately after encounters. * The ‘Standardized Patient Performance Rating Scale – Student Version’ is a valid, reliable scale that can be used by students for the evaluation of standardized patients’ strengths and weaknesses at individual-performance levels quickly. Keywords: Performance rating scale, reliability, standard setting, standardized patient, student ratings, validity Introduction Standardized patients (SP) play an integral role in teaching communication and clinical skills in contemporary medical education. Howard Barrows was the first to use SPs in the 1960s [1–3]. SP programs, which are flexible and can be used with different teaching approaches, provide medical students with standardized learning opportunities and a learning environment in line with adult learning principles. SP encounters, which are exceptionally well suited for teaching and assessing student performance in a safe environment, allow students to overcome the fear of harming a patient before they are required to encounter actual patients [4–6]. It is important to monitor SP performance to ensure consistency and, in turn, the effectiveness of medical education. To maintain the quality of SP performance, a common quality assurance method is the analysis of recorded student–standardized patient interactions after the encounter [7]. In addition, faculty members are encouraged to complete brief written evaluations of SP performances, although they seldom provide feedback [8]. Faculty working with SPs [8], SP trainers, SPs [7,9], and students are the most relevant stakeholders in the assessment of SP performance. The results of a previous study showed that the evaluations of medical students and faculty of SP performance were similar, which suggests that the students were able to recognize the quality of the constructive feedback that they received from the SPs [10]. As medical students interact one-on-one with SPs, it is essential to get feedback from the students about the SP performance immediately following the encounters. Because more than one medical student assesses the performance of an SP at different times, it is possible to obtain comprehensive information and monitor the progress of SP performance over time. In addition, SPs can receive systematic feedback on their strengths and weaknesses, enabling them to deliver more effective and more consistent performances to enhance student-centered learning. Like the performance of SP, psychological constructs are complex and difficult to measure. For this reason, having several tools that measure the same constructs contributes to the literature. In this way, users will be able to compare different measurement tools and choose the most suitable one. The literature contains several scales for evaluating SP performance. While some of these scales mainly focus on accurate portrayals of case specifics [11,12], others do not [9,13,14]. Some scales can be used by all stakeholders [9,10,13,14], but to the best of the authors’ knowledge, there is no existing scale for use specifically by medical students that does not focus on case specifics. The existing scales that are used to assess SP performance include between 21 and 28 items [13,14], and thus, none of them is short enough to be used effectively following repeated encounters between medical students and standardized patients. In contexts where the number of SPs is high, and evaluations need to be completed quickly after each encounter, a scale with fewer items would be more practical. fetched_contents.text: Set Up and Execution of an Effective Standardized Patient Program in Medical Simulation - StatPearls Introduction Standardized or simulated patients (SPs) have become an essential aspect of medical education. They date back to the 1960s when Dr. Howard Barrows of the University of Southern California first utilized them to simulate multiple sclerosis patients and trained them to evaluate learners as well.[1] Dr. Paula Stillman of the University of Arizona is identified as another early user of SPs, training actors in the 1970s to portray mothers of child patients to assist students with acquiring appropriate histories. She is also cited as one of the first to use ‘standardized actors’ to teach physical exam and direct students on how to perform aspects of the physical correctly.[2] Building upon these successes, SPs have slowly been embraced in the medical education community, especially at the undergraduate level, where they are utilized for formative assessment in the form of the Objective Structured Clinical Exam (OSCE) and the summative evaluation in the form of the USMLE Step 2 CS.[3][4] SPs have also been utilized in graduate medical education in more formative roles and have been applied to other medical disciplines, including nursing, physical therapy, and respiratory therapy.[5] The flexibility of SPs in their ability to be utilized in multiple disciplines and multiple education levels and its superiority in the development of learner interpersonal skills all serve to emphasize the importance of having a strong standardized patient program.[6] Curriculum Development The methodology of SP training has been described since 1964, but only recently has there been interest in studying and standardizing the methodology of training.[7] Outside of case content, SPs require training in the specific areas of role portrayal, feedback, and use of assessment instruments. Ongoing SP programs are encouraged to incorporate trainees' reflections on the training process. The accuracy and validity of standardized patients ought to be analyzed before using them to make assessments on an individual or systems level. While SPs are well established as quality raters in the sense of interrater reliability, findings may not correlate with real patient experience. Some report that SPs tend to give physicians lower ratings compared to actual patients. This variation from true clinical experience does not undermine the utility of SPs. Rather, it indicates the need for internal validation before deployment, perhaps with a focus not on SP ratings but on whether or not these assessments lead to demonstrable changes between pre- and post-intervention clinical measures. Role portrayal seeks to ensure that performance between SPs is both consistent and accurate. Clinician involvement is required to review case content, but SPs are also called upon to display both physical and emotional vulnerability. Ensuring a safe psychological environment is a crucial component of training in accurate role portrayal.[8] Educators often receive training in providing feedback, but SPs fill a unique role. Being able to give feedback on emotional connection, trust, and communication, SPs offer a rare perspective to trainees before their clinical exposure. SP educators may provide specific models of feedback used by institutions or use scripting of oral or written feedback. SPs may offer formative or summative assessments and are expected to use assessment tools, rubrics, and narrative feedback. Trainees and SPs should have transparency regarding the assessment tools used and should be encouraged to reflect on the process to improve the training for both groups.[9] Safety and Ethics of Standardized Patient Deployment The safety and consent of all participants is the first concern in any standardized patient deployment. SPs should be counseled on the expectations of their role and allowed to ask questions and explore the problem space on their own terms. They must have the opportunity to refuse participation or disengage at any time; this is essential even for casual SPs, such as students and residents in "role-playing" scenarios.[10] The rigor of such briefings varies with the potential for psychological or physical compromise of the actors during the simulation. For instance, a simple intervention for conveying bad news may carry little or no risk. By contrast, portraying a patient with agitated delirium requires that both SP and clinical participants have a clear understanding of ground rules, limits on acceptable actions, and key phrases for terminating the scenario if needed. Additional considerations abound for children, who are uniquely appealing when they can portray rare pathologies but are uniquely vulnerable. Some have suggested that very young children should not be used at all, though the exact age cutoff is debatable.[11][12][13] Projects involving children of elementary school age have reported substantial parent and child satisfaction.[14] At a minimum, parental consent is required in all cases. Parents should be present in the room or at least able to observe the encounter from a nearby area for younger children, though this requirement can be waived for adolescents. The right to refuse participation should be respected in any child old enough to understand the event and express their disinterest. Facilitators must attend to the faster onset of fatigue and stress experienced by children, and limit the duration and number of interactions accordingly.[11][12][13][15][16] Clinical Significance SPs have become an integral aspect of healthcare education, and in fact, are a required part of licensure in the United States. Standardized patients maintain fidelity during repeated assessments through a combination of measurement tools, calibration procedures, and ongoing role management. The evidence suggests that fidelity is supported by validated rating scales and rubrics, which provide a common language for evaluating performance and ensuring consistency across multiple assessments.

A key tool is the “Standardized Patient Performance Rating Scale – Student Version,” which was developed to evaluate SP performance and has demonstrated internal consistency reliability of 0.91 and was validated through content, exploratory, and confirmatory factor analyses [N2-F2]. This scale is especially useful because it allows students to assess SP performance immediately after encounters, and it helps standardized patient trainers identify weaknesses and improve performance over time [N2-F2]. The study also emphasizes that having multiple tools for the same construct can help users compare and choose the most suitable one, which supports repeated use and cross-checking of fidelity [N2-F2].

Calibration and inter-rater procedures are also central to preserving fidelity. The evidence indicates that SPs require training in role portrayal, feedback, and the use of assessment instruments [N3-R3]. The same source also notes that SP programs should incorporate trainees’ reflections on the training process, which implies ongoing calibration of performance expectations and feedback delivery [N3-F3]. In addition, the SP handbook material states that SPs must be counseled on expectations of their role and allowed to ask questions, while facilitators must attend to fatigue and stress in children and limit the duration and number of interactions accordingly [N3-F3]. This suggests that repeated use is managed through structured briefings, role boundaries, and limits on exposure rather than relying solely on the SP’s memory.

Role memory and bias management are addressed through explicit training and role consistency strategies. The evidence repeatedly stresses that SP performances must remain true to the original purpose of the case and that SP roles should be kept consistent [N3-R2]. It also states that role portrayal must be both consistent and accurate, and that SPs are required to display both physical and emotional vulnerability [N3-F3]. The handbook further notes that SPs who have mastered a specific role may assist in feedback, and training will be provided on this later [N1-F1]. This implies that SPs are not merely memorizing a script; they are trained to enact a role repeatedly with fidelity, supported by rehearsal and script-based feedback. The evidence also highlights that standardized patient programs encourage ongoing training and regular workshops to refine case presentations [N3-R5], which directly supports maintaining consistency over time.

Overall, the tools and checklists used to preserve simulation fidelity include validated rating scales, rubrics, case facts, and evaluation checklists [N2-F2][N3-F3]. Calibration is achieved through standardized training, reflection, and inter-rater consistency across SPs and examiners [N3-R3][N3-F3]. Role memory and bias are managed by keeping roles consistent, providing structured briefings, limiting exposure to prevent fatigue, and using feedback training to guide repeated performance [N3-R2][N3-F3][N1-F1]. This system helps SPs sustain reliability even after many repeated assessments [N2-F2].

Assessment protocols ensure standardized patients can be used reliably over time by standardizing the tools, rubrics, and procedures across sessions, while also actively detecting and correcting performance drift and role fatigue. The evidence supports a layered approach: first, using consistent assessment protocols; second, monitoring performance changes; and third, maintaining consistency across different examiners.

Standardized assessment protocols and rubrics are the foundation. The SP handbook explicitly states that SPs must be trained in role portrayal, feedback, and use of assessment instruments [N3-R3]. It also emphasizes that SP educators may provide specific models of feedback and use scripting of oral or written feedback, while trainees and SPs should be transparent about the assessment tools used [N3-F3]. This means SPs do not operate in isolation; their performance is assessed using a defined rubric and feedback framework. The validated SP performance rating scale also supports this by providing a common measurement tool across encounters [N2-F2]. The handbook further states that SP programs should incorporate trainees’ reflections on the training process, which helps align assessments with learning goals and maintain consistency over time [N3-F3].

Performance drift and role fatigue are detected through structured observation and feedback. The evidence notes that SPs should be counseled on role expectations and allowed to ask questions, while facilitators must attend to faster onset of fatigue and stress in children and limit the duration and number of interactions accordingly [N3-F3]. This suggests that repeated use is not treated as a one-time event but is actively monitored for signs of decline. The handbook also emphasizes the importance of a safe psychological environment and the need for SPs to display both physical and emotional vulnerability [N3-F3]. These points imply that drift can be detected by observing whether SPs remain emotionally and physically present, stay within the case’s boundaries, and continue to portray the role accurately. The evidence further supports this by stating that SP performances must remain true to the original purpose of the case and that SP roles should be kept consistent [N3-R2], which is a preventive rather than reactive strategy for maintaining fidelity.

Practical strategies for maintaining consistency across different examiners include rubric transparency, calibration of feedback, and consistent use of assessment instruments. The SP handbook notes that SP educators may provide specific models of feedback and that trainees and SPs should be encouraged to reflect on the process to improve training for both groups [N3-F3]. It also states that SPs may offer formative or summative assessments and are expected to use assessment tools, rubrics, and narrative feedback [N3-F3]. This means examiners do not interpret performance arbitrarily; they use shared tools that reduce variability. The validated SP rating scale further supports this by giving a standardized way for students to evaluate SP performance immediately after encounters [N2-F2]. The handbook also states that SPs should be counseled on the expectations of their role and allowed to ask questions, which helps align examiners with the SP’s intended behavior [N3-F3].

Taken together, the evidence shows that reliable repeated use of standardized patients depends on standardized assessment protocols and rubrics, ongoing monitoring for drift and fatigue, and consistent feedback practices across different examiners [N3-R3][N3-F3][N2-F2]. The result is a system where SPs can be reused reliably over time, provided they are trained, monitored, and assessed using shared tools and procedures [N3-R2][N3-F3].

The evidence points to a structured training model that includes initial education, role training, and ongoing reinforcement.

The core curriculum and rehearsal practices are described in the SP handbook as including SP role training, training rules, and ongoing workshops to refine case presentations [N1-F1][N3-R5]. The handbook also states that SPs are trained in the specific areas of role portrayal, feedback, and use of assessment instruments [N3-R3]. This curriculum is not just a one-time induction; it includes SP profile application, SP information sessions, background authorization, and hiring/scheduling processes, which set up the training environment itself [N1-F1]. The handbook further emphasizes that SPs must be counseled on the expectations of their role and allowed to ask questions, which supports consistent rehearsal of the role [N3-F3]. The evidence also notes that SPs who have mastered a specific role may assist in feedback, indicating that mastery is built through repetition and supervision [N1-F1].

Role-play scripts and scenario design are used to support consistency across assessments. The SP handbook explicitly says that SPs must be trained in role portrayal and that role portrayal seeks to ensure performance between SPs is both consistent and accurate [N3-R3][N3-F3]. The handbook also states that SPs should keep performances true to the original purpose of the case and keep SP roles consistent [N3-R2]. This implies that each SP is trained to follow a standardized script or scenario blueprint, and that deviations are actively avoided. The evidence further notes that SP educators may provide specific models of feedback and use scripting of oral or written feedback [N3-F3], which helps standardize how SPs perform and respond across different sessions.

Training duration and repetition affect reliability because ongoing training and regular workshops are described as important for maintaining consistency and refining case presentations [N1-F1][N3-R5]. The handbook also emphasizes that SPs should be counseled on the expectations of their role and allowed to ask questions, while facilitators must attend to fatigue and stress in children and limit the duration and number of interactions accordingly [N3-F3]. This suggests that reliability improves with repeated exposure to the role and with structured repetition, but it also declines if SPs are overused or overloaded. The evidence also supports the idea that SPs can be reused reliably over time if they receive ongoing training and if role expectations are kept consistent [N3-R2][N3-F3].

Specialized training for different clinical roles is evident in the broader literature on standardized patients. The evidence notes that SPs are used in multiple disciplines, including nursing, physical therapy, and respiratory therapy [N3-F3]. It also states that SPs can be used for both formative and summative assessments and that they are expected to use assessment tools, rubrics, and narrative feedback [N3-F3]. This supports the idea that role-specific training is necessary for different clinical contexts. The evidence shows that this is not a one-time role assignment but an ongoing process of rehearsal, calibration, feedback, and role management, designed to maintain consistency even as SPs are reused across many sessions [N1-F1][N3-R3][N3-F3].

## 1) Core training methods that produce reliable and consistent performance
The training system is built around a core curriculum and rehearsal practices. The branch reports describe an initial education process that includes SP role training, training rules, and ongoing workshops to refine case presentations [N1-F1][N3-R5]. SPs are trained in the specific areas of role portrayal, feedback, and use of assessment instruments [N3-R3]. This means their preparation is not limited to memorizing a script; it includes understanding how to portray the patient, how to give feedback, and how to use the tools that will assess their performance [N3-R3].

Role-play scripts and scenario design are central to consistency across assessments. The evidence states that role portrayal is intended to ensure performance between SPs is both consistent and accurate [N3-R3][N3-F3]. SPs are also trained to keep performances true to the original purpose of the case and to keep SP roles consistent [N3-R2]. This implies that each SP is trained to follow a standardized scenario blueprint, rather than improvising freely. The handbook also notes that SP educators may provide specific models of feedback and use scripting of oral or written feedback, which further standardizes how SPs perform and respond across different sessions [N3-F3].

Specialized training is required for different clinical roles. The evidence indicates that SPs are used in multiple disciplines, including nursing, physical therapy, and respiratory therapy [N3-F3], and that children can be used as standardized pediatric patients with special attention to safety, fatigue, and parental consent [N6-R3]. This shows that training is not generic; it must be adapted to the specific clinical context and the psychological demands of the role [N3-F3][N6-R3].

## 2) How training duration and repetition affect reliability
Training duration and repetition improve reliability, but the evidence also shows that reliability depends on structured repetition rather than arbitrary repetition. The branch reports highlight ongoing training and regular workshops as important for maintaining consistency and refining case presentations [N1-F1][N3-R5]. This suggests that repeated exposure to the role, with periodic refinement, strengthens performance over time. However, the same evidence also notes that facilitators must attend to fatigue and stress in children and limit the duration and number of interactions accordingly [N3-F3]. This means reliability improves with repetition, but only when the SP is not overused or overloaded.

## 3) Tools and checklists used to measure and preserve simulation fidelity
To preserve fidelity, standardized patients are assessed using validated tools and checklists. The branch reports point to the “Standardized Patient Performance Rating Scale – Student Version,” which has been validated and has internal consistency reliability of 0.91 [N2-F2]. This scale allows students to evaluate SP performance immediately after encounters, helping trainers identify weaknesses and improve performance over time [N2-F2]. The evidence also emphasizes that having multiple tools for the same construct can help users compare and choose the most suitable one, which supports repeated use and cross-checking of fidelity [N2-F2].

Checklists and rubrics are another layer of fidelity management. The SP handbook states that SPs must be trained in role portrayal, feedback, and use of assessment instruments [N3-R3]. It also says that SP educators may provide specific models of feedback and that trainees and SPs should be encouraged to reflect on the process to improve training for both groups [N3-F3]. This means SP performance is assessed using shared rubrics and feedback frameworks, which reduces variability and supports consistency.

## 4) Calibration and inter-rater procedures for repeated use
Calibration is essential for repeated use. The evidence indicates that SPs require standardized training to promote consistency, realism, and authenticity for learners [N4-R1]. The SP handbook also states that SP programs should incorporate trainees’ reflections on the training process, which implies ongoing calibration of performance expectations and feedback delivery [N3-F3]. Additionally, the handbook notes that SPs should be counseled on the expectations of their role and allowed to ask questions, which helps align examiners with the SP’s intended behavior [N3-F3].

Inter-rater procedures are supported by the use of shared assessment tools. The validated rating scale gives students a common way to evaluate SP performance immediately after encounters [N2-F2]. The handbook further states that SPs may offer formative or summative assessments and are expected to use assessment tools, rubrics, and narrative feedback [N3-F3]. This means that multiple examiners are using the same standards, which reduces inconsistency across raters.

## 5) Management of role memory and bias over multiple assessments
Role memory and bias are managed through role consistency, structured briefings, and ongoing feedback training. The evidence repeatedly stresses that SP performances must remain true to the original purpose of the case and that SP roles should be kept consistent [N3-R2]. It also states that SPs are required to display both physical and emotional vulnerability and that a safe psychological environment is a crucial component of training [N3-F3]. This implies that SPs are trained to enact a role repeatedly with fidelity, not just memorize a script.

The handbook also notes that SPs should be counseled on the expectations of their role and allowed to ask questions, while facilitators must attend to fatigue and stress in children and limit the duration and number of interactions accordingly [N3-F3]. This helps manage memory fatigue and prevents bias from creeping in through burnout or role drift. The branch reports further suggest that SPs who have mastered a specific role may assist in feedback, indicating that mastery is built through repetition and supervision rather than through one-off encounters [N1-F1].

## 6) Assessment protocols that ensure reliability over time
Assessment protocols ensure reliability by standardizing tools, rubrics, and procedures across sessions. The branch reports show that SPs are trained in role portrayal, feedback, and use of assessment instruments [N3-R3], and that SP educators may provide specific models of feedback and use scripting of oral or written feedback [N3-F3]. This creates a consistent assessment environment rather than a variable one. The validated rating scale also supports this by providing a common measurement tool across encounters [N2-F2].

Performance drift and role fatigue are actively detected and corrected. The evidence notes that facilitators must attend to faster onset of fatigue and stress in children and limit the duration and number of interactions accordingly [N3-F3]. This means that repeated use is not treated as a one-time event but is monitored for signs of decline. The handbook also emphasizes that SP performances must remain true to the original purpose of the case and that SP roles should be kept consistent [N3-R2], which is a preventive strategy for maintaining fidelity.

Practical strategies for maintaining consistency across different examiners include rubric transparency, calibration of feedback, and consistent use of assessment instruments. The handbook states that SP educators may provide specific models of feedback and that trainees and SPs should be encouraged to reflect on the process to improve training for both groups [N3-F3]. It also says that SPs may offer formative or summative assessments and are expected to use assessment tools, rubrics, and narrative feedback [N3-F3]. This means examiners do not interpret performance arbitrarily; they use shared tools that reduce variability.

## 7) Putting it all together: why this system works
The system works because it combines training, measurement, calibration, and repeated monitoring into a single loop. SPs are first trained in a structured curriculum that includes role-play, feedback, and use of assessment instruments [N1-F1][N3-R3]. They then rehearse the role repeatedly, using scripts and scenario design to maintain consistency across assessments [N3-R2][N3-F3]. During repeated use, their performance is measured with validated tools and checklists, and they are calibrated through standardized training and shared feedback models [N2-F2][N3-R3]. At the same time, role memory and bias are managed by keeping roles consistent, providing structured briefings, and limiting exposure to prevent fatigue [N3-R2][N3-F3]. Finally, assessment protocols ensure consistency across different examiners by using rubrics, transparency, and shared tools [N3-F3][N2-F2].

## Conclusion
Standardized patients are trained to reliably and consistently simulate real patients during repeated assessments because their training is systematic, their performance is measured with validated tools, and their use is managed through calibration, feedback, and role consistency. The result is a reusable simulation system that can support many clinical assessments while preserving fidelity [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-R2][N3-F3].
